items: [A | guideline supported] ACIP recommends a one-time Tdap dose for adults who have never received Tdap, followed by a Td booster every 10 years after Tdap. - PMID:29702631

[A | guideline supported] The EASL-EASD-EASO 2024 guideline recommends case-finding for MASLD with fibrosis, using non-invasive tests, in individuals with cardiometabolic risk factors, abnormal liver enzymes and/or radiological steatosis. It places particular emphasis on type 2 diabetes or obesity with additional metabolic risk factors. - PMID:38851997, PMID:38869512

[A | guideline supported] The EASL-EASD-EASO guideline endorses a stepwise approach for ruling advanced fibrosis in or out: a blood-based score such as FIB-4 first, then imaging such as transient elastography. - PMID:38851997

[B | guideline supported] For hepatocellular injury, the ACG guideline recommends: - testing for viral hepatitis A, B and C; - assessing for fatty liver disease and alcohol-related liver disease; - screening for hemochromatosis, autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson's disease and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency; - taking a history of prescribed and over-the-counter medicines. - PMID:27995906

[B | guideline supported] For adults aged 40-59 years with a 10-year CVD risk of 10% or more, starting low-dose aspirin for primary prevention is an individual decision with only a small net benefit. Persons not at increased bleeding risk are more likely to benefit. The USPSTF recommends against starting aspirin at 60 or older. (verified with caveat) - PMID:35471505

[B | guideline supported] The USPSTF recommends against beta carotene or vitamin E supplements for preventing cardiovascular disease or cancer. Evidence for multivitamins and other single or paired nutrient supplements is insufficient (I statement). (verified with caveat) - PMID:35727271

[B | guideline supported] The 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline (now superseded) recommended checking adherence and response with a repeat lipid panel 4-12 weeks after starting a statin or changing the dose. Testing was then repeated every 3-12 months as needed. Response was defined as the percentage fall in LDL-C from baseline. - PMID:30586774

[B | guideline supported] In primary prevention, the 2018 guideline aimed for at least a 30% LDL-C reduction when a statin is indicated. It aimed for at least 50% when 10-year ASCVD risk is 20% or more. - PMID:30586774

[B | guideline supported] In the EASL-EASD-EASO guideline, MASLD requires hepatic steatosis plus at least one cardiometabolic risk factor. Listed risk factors include BMI ≥25 kg/m2 (≥23 in Asian ethnicity), prediabetes by fasting glucose 5.6-6.9 mmol/L, blood pressure ≥130/85 mmHg, and triglyceride or HDL criteria, either of which can be met by lipid-lowering treatment. (verified with caveat) - PMID:38851997, PMID:38852583

[B | evidence supported] Lp(a) elevation is common in South Asians: about 20% of MASALA participants had Lp(a) ≥50 mg/dL. Levels varied modestly by country of origin, but the Lp(a)-ASCVD association did not differ across South Asian subgroups. - PMID:42868967

[B | evidence supported] In a multiethnic primary-prevention cohort that included South Asian Surinamese participants, Lp(a) was independently associated with incident ASCVD. The relative-risk gradient was consistent across ethnic groups, and absolute risk was about 3-fold higher in South Asian Surinamese participants. Adding Lp(a) and hsCRP to a clinical model improved discrimination only modestly. - PMID:42340290

[B | guideline supported] The USPSTF recommends screening for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes in adults aged 35-70 with overweight or obesity, and recommends offering or referring those with prediabetes to effective preventive interventions (B recommendation, moderate net benefit). (verified with caveat) - PMID:34427594

[B | guideline supported] The USPSTF systematic review found no significant mortality benefit from screening trials, and evidence on harms of screening was limited. The recommendation rests mainly on benefits of treating screen-detected prediabetes: lifestyle interventions reduced diabetes incidence (pooled RR 0.78) and metformin did likewise (pooled RR 0.73). (verified with caveat) - PMID:34427595

[B | evidence supported] In a large Chinese cohort, FPG-defined prediabetes (ADA or WHO criteria) was not significantly associated with all-cause or CVD mortality. HbA1c- or 2hPG-defined prediabetes was associated with modestly higher mortality. - PMID:42063461

[C | evidence supported] Diabetes diagnosis relies on biochemical criteria from fasting glucose, oral glucose tolerance testing and HbA1c, as summarised for Austrian Diabetes Association recommendations. The specific thresholds are not shown in the provided abstract. - PMID:27052219

[C | guideline supported] The ACG guideline names ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin as the core liver chemistries. It defines hepatocellular injury as disproportionate elevation of AST and ALT relative to alkaline phosphatase, and says the degree of AST/ALT elevation guides further evaluation. AST should therefore be read together with ALT and alkaline phosphatase, not alone. (verified with caveat) - PMID:27995906

[C | guideline supported] The ACG guideline states that an elevated ALT is associated with increased liver-related mortality. It gives a healthy normal ALT range of 29-33 IU/l for males and says levels above this should be assessed. The supplied sources give no equivalent AST threshold. - PMID:27995906

[C | emerging] The EASL MASLD screening algorithm, as described in the Sri Lankan study, has two steps: FIB-4 (calculated from age, AST, ALT and platelet count) first, then vibration-controlled transient elastography for patients likely to have significant fibrosis. In a South Asian cohort with ultrasound-confirmed MASLD, FIB-4 had an external-validation AUC of 0.728. Machine-learning models using the same variables plus clinical factors reached AUCs of 0.781-0.795. - PMID:42784575

[C | evidence supported] In UK primary care, AST was the main limiting factor for calculating FIB-4 in people with recorded MASLD. People of South Asian ethnicity were over-represented among MASLD diagnoses but had the lowest FIB-4 availability. Recorded MASLD was associated with higher prevalence of hypertension and type 2 diabetes. - PMID:42724572

[C | evidence supported] Colorectal cancer screening is recommended for average-risk adults aged 45-75 years, which includes this 58-year-old man unless he has higher-risk features such as adenomatous polyps, inflammatory bowel disease or a family history. First-line modalities include stool-based tests, CT colonography, flexible sigmoidoscopy and colonoscopy. - PMID:40961305

[C | evidence supported] Syphilis screening recommendations in this review target sexually active people aged 15-44 years, and annually for those at increased risk. A 58-year-old man falls outside the routine age band, so screening would depend on individual risk factors that are not documented. - PMID:41100079

[C | evidence supported] Hypertension-related cerebrovascular damage, including early microangiopathic changes, is best diagnosed by MRI, which supports considering a neurological/cerebrovascular domain in hypertension. The source does not say that every patient with hypertension needs imaging or cognitive testing. - PMID:21191547

[C | emerging] A CKD-specific guidance document proposes routine cognitive screening (MMSE and/or MoCA) integrated into the care of CKD patients. This is indirect evidence for the cognitive domain and applies to CKD, not to essential hypertension alone. - PMID:40235626

[C | evidence supported] A review of the 2026 ACC/AHA guideline reports three changes relevant here. It reintroduces explicit lipid targets. It reports LDL-C goals below 70 mg/dL for high-risk and below 55 mg/dL for very-high-risk patients, in line with the 2025 ESC/EAS update. It replaces the pooled cohort equations with PREVENT-ASCVD, defining high risk as a 10-year risk of 10% or more. The review also says CAC may guide both LDL-C and non-HDL-C goals, but no numeric non-HDL-C target appears in the excerpt. - PMID:42795336

[C | guideline supported] The 2026 guideline's scope covers monitoring of dyslipidemia, including elevated lipoprotein(a). A related study states that Lp(a) testing is recommended for all adults. - PMID:41824590, PMID:42965161

[C | evidence supported] Guidance disagrees on the lower HbA1c limit of the sub-diabetic risk range (5.7% / 39 mmol/mol versus 6.0% / 42 mmol/mol). Diabetes risk rises continuously below the diagnostic threshold rather than at a single biological cut point. - PMID:42355858

[C | emerging] The review proposes a tiered interpretation: HbA1c 5.7-6.4% supports broad, low-intensity preventive advice, and HbA1c 6.0-6.4% (especially 6.2-6.4%, or combined HbA1c and fasting glucose abnormality) identifies higher near-term risk and supports prioritising structured prevention and closer follow-up. - PMID:42355858

[C | evidence supported] A narrative review recommends screening adults older than 40 years and other high-risk individuals for diabetes using fasting plasma glucose and/or HbA1c. It does not specify a rescreening interval. - PMID:29731022

[C | evidence supported] An Australian consensus position statement (2007) recommends that, once prediabetes is established, glycaemia be followed with a formal 75 g OGTT, initially annually and then at an individualised frequency. It states there is no role for routine HbA1c testing in prediabetes. - PMID:17484708

[C | evidence supported] Management of prediabetes includes addressing cardiovascular risk factors (lipids, blood pressure, smoking). For overweight or obese people with prediabetes, intensive lifestyle intervention is recommended to help prevent progression to diabetes. - PMID:17484708

[C | evidence supported] Different glycaemic definitions (FPG-defined, HbA1c-defined, IGT) identify overlapping but distinct metabolic states. Men predominantly show raised fasting glucose, whereas women more often show impaired glucose tolerance. - PMID:30980153, PMID:42666695

[C | evidence supported] Prediabetes tends to progress to type 2 diabetes over time, and sustained recovery is uncommon without intervention. This underpins the rationale for follow-up testing. - PMID:41115173

[C | evidence supported] Under South Asian-modified NCEP criteria, as applied in a South Indian cohort, the abdominal obesity component is waist circumference ≥90 cm in men (≥80 cm in women). Metabolic syndrome requires any three of five components. - PMID:42237830

[C | evidence supported] Both the NCEP-ATP III and IDF metabolic syndrome definitions adopt ethnic-specific waist cut points. IDF requires central obesity as a prerequisite, whereas NCEP-ATP III weights each component equally. Asian data reportedly favour the NCEP-ATP III approach. - PMID:18296297

[C | evidence supported] Asians, including South Asians, appear to have greater cardiometabolic risk at lower BMI and lower waist circumference than other populations. This is the stated rationale for lower ethnic-specific waist thresholds. - PMID:18296297, PMID:18682591, PMID:42461970

[C | emerging] The optimal ethnic-specific waist cut points remain uncertain. Reviewers note a lack of studies in Asian-descent groups and suggest that international cutoffs may misclassify risk in South Asian populations. - PMID:19639001, PMID:42461970

[C | emerging] A 2026 narrative review applies standard age-adjusted FIB-4 cut-offs: <1.3 under 65 years or <2.0 at 65 or older to rule out, and >2.67 as high risk. For South Asian patients it states a lower rule-out cut-off of <1.0, attributed to a 2025 Global Consensus. The indeterminate band for South Asians under 65 is therefore 1.0–2.67. - PMID:42533336

[C | emerging] In a Sri Lankan tertiary VCTE-registry external validation cohort (n=430) with MASLD on ultrasound, FIB-4 detected significant fibrosis with an AUC of 0.728, PPV 0.719 and NPV 0.696. Machine-learning models using the individual FIB-4 components plus clinical variables performed better (AUC 0.781–0.795). - PMID:42784575

[C | emerging] In UK primary care, South Asian people with recorded MASLD had the lowest availability of FIB-4 components. Among those with a calculable score, fewer South Asian than White individuals fell into the indeterminate or high-risk categories. This is an association; the source does not establish whether it reflects less fibrosis or lower FIB-4 sensitivity in South Asians. - PMID:42724572

[C | evidence supported] FIB-4 can miss clinically important liver disease in general populations. In a multinational cohort that included Indian centres, 26% of non-cirrhotic MASLD-related HCC cases had a low FIB-4 (<1.3, or <2 if over 65). In a US insured cohort, FIB-4 ≥2.67 had 41.3% sensitivity and 91.0% specificity for diagnosed cirrhosis. - PMID:38074510, PMID:39462858

[C | emerging] A 2024 South Asian clinical review found no ancestry-specific guidelines for diagnosing or managing MASLD. It also noted that general guidelines may not apply because South Asians differ in phenotype, including lean/'thin-fat' MASLD. - PMID:39498281

[C | emerging] In a large MASLD/type 2 diabetes cohort, elevated alkaline phosphatase (≥120 U/L) independently modified FIB-4-associated risk of major adverse liver outcomes. This suggests FIB-4 interpretation may be refined by cholestatic enzyme status. - PMID:42966709

[C | hypothesis] A mechanistic review proposes structured liver function monitoring, along with pharmacogenomic considerations such as SLCO1B1 and CYP3A4, as part of a personalised approach to atorvastatin safety. This is a proposal, not a guideline recommendation. - PMID:41784742

[C | evidence supported] Narrative reviews report that contemporary guidance recommends stepwise FIB-4-based assessment in at-risk groups. They name type 2 diabetes, obesity with additional metabolic risk, established steatosis and persistently abnormal liver tests as these groups. AASLD guidance is cited as warning that normal aminotransferases do not exclude significant fibrosis. - PMID:42597408, PMID:42942568
[C | evidence supported] FIB-4 is calculated from age, AST, ALT and platelet count. - PMID:42942568
[C | emerging] In a Saudi primary-care cohort with MASLD, diabetes, male sex and waist circumference were independently associated with significant fibrosis (liver stiffness ≥8 kPa). - PMID:42942568

[C | guideline supported] The 2018 ACC/AHA cholesterol guideline lists Lp(a) ≥50 mg/dL or ≥125 nmol/L as a risk-enhancing factor, to be measured only in selected individuals. It does not recommend universal testing, either in the general population or specifically in South Asians. South Asian ethnicity is separately listed as a risk-enhancing factor for intermediate-risk adults aged 40-75 without diabetes. (verified with caveat) - PMID:30586774

[C | evidence supported] Reviews describe Lp(a) as a causal, largely genetically determined ASCVD risk factor. Cardiovascular risk thresholds are reported as >30-50 mg/dL (75-125 nmol/L). However, Lp(a) is currently not a treatment target, and measurement should use well-validated, traceable assays. - PMID:33236085, PMID:39302109

[C | emerging] South Asian-specific data on optimal lipid parameters, including Lp(a), and on the best risk-prediction tools are limited. Major risk scores classify South Asian patients very differently and may miss most people who go on to have events. - PMID:33438542, PMID:42470426

[C | evidence supported] A 2026 European update on diabetes screening lists risk-based criteria for asymptomatic adults: BMI ≥25 kg/m2 (23 for Asian origin) plus one or more risk factors; otherwise screening from age 35. Hypertension (≥130/80 mm Hg or on antihypertensive therapy) is among the listed risk factors, and known prediabetes should be screened annually. - PMID:42162460

[C | evidence supported] Key screening tests for dysglycaemia are fasting plasma glucose and HbA1c. ADA and USPSTF advise opportunistic screening every 3 years. There is no direct trial evidence that screening itself is effective. - PMID:34399951

[C | emerging] A narrative cardiology review lists age among risk factors for vascular cognitive impairment and suggests enquiring about cognitive concerns in older patients. This is a clinician-oriented suggestion, not a guideline recommendation for formal screening, and the patient is 58, so he may fall outside 'older patients'. - PMID:41498479

[C | emerging] The same review rates mid-life hypertension as an established and strong risk factor for vascular cognitive impairment and dementia, and advises early detection and treatment according to guidelines. It does not recommend baseline cognitive testing or imaging. - PMID:41498479

[C | emerging] Brain MRI is positioned as a diagnostic step once a cognitive syndrome has been identified, to establish a vascular cause. It is not described as a screening test for asymptomatic hypertensive adults. - PMID:41498479

[C | emerging] Hypertension is described as a modifiable vascular risk factor for cognitive decline and dementia, and cognitive impairment is described as common among patients with hypertension. This is a scoping-review statement, and it does not establish a screening recommendation. - PMID:42746159

[C | emerging] Mendelian randomization suggests blood pressure causally relates to white matter hyperintensity volume, including in people without clinical hypertension. This is genetic evidence of mechanism, not evidence that imaging screening improves outcomes. - PMID:33293549

[C | emerging] Reviews on cerebral small vessel disease report that intensive blood pressure control is the mainstay of prevention. One review says intensive lowering reduces white matter hyperintensity progression and delays cognitive impairment. This supports blood pressure management over screening, and the targets are not stated in the excerpts. - PMID:31142635, PMID:36575578

[C | evidence supported] Per a secondary review, the 2026 ACC/AHA guideline reintroduces treatment goals for LDL-C, non-HDL-C and apoB in primary prevention, assigned by risk category. The numeric values for borderline and intermediate risk are not given in the provided excerpts. - PMID:42295619, PMID:42932934
[C | evidence supported] The 2026 guideline's PREVENT-ASCVD 10-year risk categories are: low <3%, borderline 3% to <5%, intermediate 5% to <10%, and high ≥10%. - PMID:42795336

[C | evidence supported] The only primary or general prevention numeric LDL-C goals in the provided sources are below 70 mg/dL for high-risk and below 55 mg/dL for very-high-risk patients. These are framed as points of convergence with ESC/EAS, not as borderline or intermediate goals. - PMID:42795336

[C | evidence supported] For very-high-risk patients with clinical ASCVD, the guideline recommends LDL-C <55 mg/dL and non-HDL-C <85 mg/dL. These are secondary prevention targets and are not applicable to borderline or intermediate primary prevention. - PMID:42709273

[C | evidence supported] Per a review, coronary artery calcium (CAC) has a structured reclassification role in the 2026 guideline and may guide both LDL-C and non-HDL-C goals. In primary prevention, the goal could therefore shift with the CAC result. - PMID:42795336

[C | emerging] Not all 2026 guideline recommendations rest on cardiovascular outcome trials; some are extensions of observational risk prediction or surrogate lipid efficacy. Category-specific goals may therefore have mixed evidence strength. - PMID:42795336
[C | evidence supported] A narrative review reports the ADA definition of prediabetes as HbA1c 5.7-6.4%, FPG 100-125 mg/dL, or 2-hour OGTT glucose 140-199 mg/dL. - PMID:42796348

[C | evidence supported] Two FPG cut-offs, 100 mg/dL and 110 mg/dL, have been used to define IFG. FPG below 126 mg/dL with no antidiabetic treatment was used to define non-diabetic status. Mild (100-109) and advanced (110-125 mg/dL) dysglycaemia were distinguished. - PMID:19078990

[C | emerging] In hypertensive non-diabetic patients, even mildly raised FPG (100-109 mg/dL) was associated with atherogenic dyslipidaemia, obesity and a worse CHD risk profile. The role of IFG as an independent risk factor was not established. - PMID:19078990

[C | evidence supported] The NCEP ATP III metabolic syndrome criteria, as tabulated in a review, use fasting glucose of 100 mg/dL or higher (or treatment for elevated glucose) as one of five criteria. - PMID:42796348

[C | evidence supported] Risk of type 2 diabetes rises continuously below diagnostic thresholds. A combined HbA1c and fasting glucose abnormality identifies adults at higher near-term risk than either alone. - PMID:42355858

[C | evidence supported] Per the ADA criteria tabulated in a 2021 review, adults with prediabetes should be retested annually. All other screened patients should be rescreened at a minimum of 3-year intervals, with more frequent testing considered depending on initial results and risk status. - PMID:34399951

[C | evidence supported] Hypertension is explicitly listed as a risk factor that, together with overweight or obesity, qualifies an adult for diabetes screening under ADA criteria. ADA uses a lower BMI threshold for Asian Americans. - PMID:34399951

[C | evidence supported] The Endocrine Society, as summarised, recommends testing people with prediabetes at least annually. Adults aged 40–75 without atherosclerotic CVD or T2DM who have at least one risk factor should be screened every 3 years. USPSTF recommends every 3 years. - PMID:34399951

[C | evidence supported] The review notes there is no trial evidence of screening effectiveness. Its overall conclusion supports opportunistic screening of asymptomatic high-risk individuals with a 3-year rescreening interval. - PMID:34399951

[C | evidence supported] The Korean Diabetes Association 2025 consensus lists hypertension (BP ≥140/90 mm Hg or use of antihypertensive medication) as a T2DM risk factor. It recommends risk-aligned screening from age 35, or from age 19 when risk factors are present. Its rescreening interval is not shown in the provided excerpt. - PMID:41243295

[C | evidence supported] Choice of rescreening test matters. Fasting plasma glucose can be affected by short-term lifestyle changes and processing error. HbA1c is more stable but can be affected by hemoglobinopathies and anemia, and is insensitive for impaired glucose tolerance. - PMID:34399951

[C | evidence supported] A South Indian study used South Asian-modified NCEP criteria for metabolic syndrome. These set the waist circumference threshold at ≥90 cm for men and ≥80 cm for women. The study describes this as NCEP-based, not as the IDF or harmonized definition, so it does not directly confirm the IDF source of the ≥90 cm threshold. - PMID:42237830

[C | evidence supported] Both NCEP-ATP III and IDF use ethnic-specific waist circumference cut points. IDF requires central obesity as a prerequisite, whereas NCEP-ATP III gives equal weight to each component. Asian data reportedly favour the newer NCEP-ATP III definition, based on similar Framingham risk scores in people identified by NCEP but not by IDF. - PMID:18296297

[C | emerging] In Nepalese adults, waist circumference and BMI had comparable, only fair-to-acceptable discrimination (AUC 0.6-0.7) for cardiometabolic conditions. Waist circumference was the only measure associated with hypertension. Discrimination exceeded 0.8 only when combined with age and sex. These were cross-sectional associations, not outcome validation. - PMID:42461970

[D | emerging] In a small prospective cohort of nondiabetic patients with newly diagnosed essential hypertension (n=106, 6 incident diabetes cases over a mean 5.9 years), baseline FPG >5.8 mmol/L and ALT >31 U/L independently predicted new-onset type 2 diabetes. Having at least 2 indicators was predictive. This is an association, not a causal or guideline finding. - PMID:19948433

[D | emerging] In a semi-urban South Indian population, metabolic syndrome (IDF 2005 Asian criteria) was present in 29.7% of adults. Increased fasting plasma glucose was found in 57.4% of those with metabolic syndrome. Systolic hypertension was the most frequent component after waist. - PMID:21510460

[D | guideline supported] Kidney function and CKD-specific pathways. Per the review, the 2026 guideline treats stage 3-4 CKD (with diabetes and HIV) as supporting LDL-lowering therapy regardless of LDL-C. KDIGO 2014 recommends a statin or statin/ezetimibe for adults aged 50 or older with eGFR <60 who are not on dialysis or transplanted. KDIGO advises against routine follow-up lipid measurement in CKD. (verified with caveat) - PMID:24552851, PMID:42795336

[D | evidence supported] NICE guidance is reported to recommend baseline LFTs before starting a statin, repeat testing within three months and at 12 months, and thereafter testing only if statin-related symptoms develop. - PMID:32313740

[D | evidence supported] US ACC/AHA guidance is reported to recommend baseline LFTs, with further testing only when clinically indicated. A 2026 case report likewise states that ACC/AHA guidelines do not require routine monitoring of liver biochemistries but advise vigilance for hepatitis symptoms, especially in high-risk patients or with supratherapeutic dosing. - PMID:32313740, PMID:42725327

[D | evidence supported] Clinically significant statin hepatotoxicity is described as rare. Transaminase elevations are reported in about 1-3% of statin users, and severe liver injury is estimated at fewer than 1 in 100,000 treated individuals. This low rate has led some clinicians to question routine LFT monitoring. - PMID:14740794, PMID:42725327

[D | emerging] Most statin-associated aminotransferase elevations are reported to occur within 12 weeks of starting, although latencies up to one year occur. On the basis of single cases, some authors recommend routine LFTs in the first few months even in asymptomatic patients. - PMID:32313740

blocks.text: Abnormal domains: cardiometabolic, hepatic

items: [D | guideline supported] A peri-operative guideline excerpt specifies how BP should be measured when considering a diagnosis of hypertension. Measure in both arms and repeat if the systolic difference is >5 mmHg. Use a validated, calibrated device and correct cuff size, with the patient seated and rested. Repeat readings and record the pulse rate and rhythm. The guideline says these methods follow the principles mandated for primary care. (verified with caveat) - PMID:41532177

[D | guideline supported] The same guideline excerpt says that for confirming hypertension in primary care, patients should be offered ambulatory BP monitoring (average of 14 daytime measurements). If that is unsuitable or not tolerated, home BP monitoring over 4-7 days is the alternative. (verified with caveat) - PMID:41532177

[C | evidence supported] A narrative review of recent hypertension guidelines (AHA/ACC, ESC/ESH, NICE) reports that updated guidelines increasingly promote out-of-office BP monitoring. They also promote individualised treatment based on overall cardiovascular risk, comorbidities and target-organ damage. This implies that assessing comorbidity and target-organ damage is part of evaluation, but the abstract does not list the specific history, examination or test elements. - PMID:42411518

[C | evidence supported] A comparison of the 2025 AHA/ACC BP guideline with HEARTS 2.0 states that the AHA/ACC guideline has broader laboratory evaluation and greater emphasis on secondary hypertension. HEARTS 2.0 includes explicit laboratory thresholds for cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic risk factors and opportunistic atrial fibrillation screening. The excerpt does not name the specific tests. - PMID:42756877

[C | evidence supported] A narrative comparison of the 2023 ESH, 2024 ESC, 2021 KDIGO and 2025 AHA/ACC guidelines reports consensus on standardized office and out-of-office BP measurement and on systematic assessment of eGFR and albuminuria with confirmation of abnormalities. This covers parts of baseline evaluation, but it comes from a review focused on CKD and is not an itemised guideline checklist. - PMID:42422469

[C | evidence supported] A review of the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline reports that its updates include broader primary aldosteronism screening and routine urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio measurement. Together with eGFR assessment, these expand target-organ and secondary-cause evaluation earlier in care. - PMID:42704524

[A | guideline supported] The Endocrine Society guideline suggests that all individuals with hypertension be screened for primary aldosteronism using aldosterone, renin and the aldosterone-to-renin ratio. This is a condition-specific screening recommendation, not an itemised initial work-up from ESC/ESH, AHA/ACC or NICE. - PMID:40658480

[C | guideline supported] The 2017 ACC/AHA synopsis lists the topics its recommendations cover, including BP classification, BP measurement and screening for secondary hypertension. The supplied abstract does not itemise the history, examination, laboratory or ECG content. - PMID:29357392

[B | guideline supported] The Endocrine Society 2025 guideline suggests screening all individuals with hypertension for primary aldosteronism with aldosterone, renin and the aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR). Further care is guided by the results. - PMID:40658480

[C | evidence supported] The AHA/ACC 2025 guideline, as summarised in a secondary review, gives a Class 1 recommendation to screen resistant hypertension for PA regardless of hypokalaemia. It gives a Class 2b recommendation to consider screening all adults with stage 2 hypertension. The ESC 2024 guideline goes further and considers screening all adults with confirmed hypertension. - PMID:41645899

[C | evidence supported] Reviews of the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline note broader laboratory evaluation, greater emphasis on secondary hypertension, and routine UACR measurement. The excerpts do not list the specific baseline tests for secondary causes, which are therefore unspecified here. UACR is described as target-organ evaluation, not as a secondary-cause test. - PMID:42704524, PMID:42756877
[C | evidence supported] Per the AHA/ACC 2025 summary, most antihypertensive medications (except MRAs) may be continued before ARR testing, which lowers barriers to testing. - PMID:41645899

[C | evidence supported] The ESC 2024 guideline is described as retaining the diagnostic threshold of 140/90 mmHg and confirming diagnosis with out-of-office or repeated office measurements. This addresses diagnosis rather than the initial work-up content. - PMID:42834368

[C | evidence supported] A secondary review states that the 2025 guideline expands screening for primary aldosteronism to all patients with stage 2 or resistant hypertension. This is one baseline or secondary-cause evaluation element, but it is not an itemised list of basic baseline tests. - PMID:41843050

[C | evidence supported] A comparative analysis notes that the 2025 guideline has broader laboratory evaluation than HEARTS 2.0 and a greater emphasis on secondary hypertension. It does not specify which laboratory tests are included. - PMID:42756877

[C | evidence supported] A secondary review states that the guideline adopts the PREVENT risk calculator, which incorporates renal function, statin use and social drivers of health. This implies that kidney function data feed into risk assessment, but it does not state which baseline tests are mandated. - PMID:41843050

[C | evidence supported] NG136 content in the supplied sources covers antihypertensive drug choice by age, ethnicity and diabetes, and caution about RAAS inhibitors in pregnancy. – of it addresses the initial assessment of target organ damage or cardiovascular risk. - PMID:40275065

[C | evidence supported] The NG136 systematic review and economic model in the supplied sources concerns diagnosis of hypertension (ambulatory vs home vs clinic BP), not assessment of target organ damage or cardiovascular risk. (verified with caveat) - PMID:32461579

[C | evidence supported] Secondary reviews of the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline report that it expanded PA screening and made UACR measurement routine. Both belong to the evaluation of secondary causes and target-organ damage. - PMID:41843050, PMID:42704524

[C | evidence supported] PA screening in the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline: Class 1 for resistant hypertension regardless of potassium, and Class 2b (consider) for all adults with stage 2 hypertension. The aldosterone-to-renin ratio is the preferred initial test. - PMID:41645899

items: [A | guideline supported] For monitoring, the 2018 AHA/ACC guideline recommends repeat lipid measurement 4 to 12 weeks after statin initiation or dose adjustment, then every 3 to 12 months as needed. Response is judged by percentage LDL-C reduction from baseline. - PMID:30586774

[B | guideline supported] The 2018 AHA/ACC guideline uses a 70 mg/dL (1.8 mmol/L) LDL-C threshold to consider adding nonstatins in very high-risk ASCVD. It also gives percentage-reduction goals for primary prevention: at least 30% if a statin is indicated, and at least 50% if 10-year risk is 20% or higher. No absolute LDL-C goal is stated for primary prevention in the excerpt. (verified with caveat) - PMID:30586774

[B | guideline supported] In the 2018 AHA/ACC guideline, elevated blood pressure is a major risk factor in the clinician-patient risk discussion. South Asian ancestry is listed as a risk-enhancing factor that favors statin therapy in intermediate-risk adults. (verified with caveat) - PMID:30586774

[B | guideline supported] The CKM guideline recommends screening intervals for glycemia by CKM stage, not by ethnicity: at least every 5 years in stage 0, every 2-3 years in stage 1, and at least annually in stage 2 and above. It does not state South Asian-specific glycemic cut-offs or intervals in the excerpt provided. - PMID:42265997

[C | emerging] Total cholesterol is the sum of LDL-C, HDL-C and a remnant (triglyceride-rich lipoprotein) fraction. A review proposes that elevated remnant cholesterol, rather than triglyceride itself, may drive atherosclerosis through cholesterol entrapment in the arterial intima. This is a mechanistic explanation and does not show causation in this patient. - PMID:21314630

[C | evidence supported] An AHA science advisory concluded that dietary cholesterol record above current average levels tends to raise total and LDL cholesterol in intervention-study meta-analyses. It advised that dietary guidance focus on healthy dietary patterns such as Mediterranean-style and DASH-style diets, rather than a specific cholesterol target. (verified with caveat) - PMID:31838890

[C | evidence supported] Diagnosis of prediabetes and diabetes rests on glycaemic criteria (fasting plasma glucose, 2 h OGTT glucose, HbA1c). A fasting glucose above the laboratory reference range therefore points towards confirmatory glycaemic testing, not a diagnosis from one value. The sources give no numeric diagnostic cut-offs. - PMID:42930797

[C | evidence supported] The triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index, computed from fasting triglycerides and fasting glucose, is described as a surrogate marker of insulin resistance. It is also associated with cardiovascular, kidney and fatty-liver disease. This is a mechanistic link between an elevated fasting glucose and insulin resistance. - PMID:39510865

[C | evidence supported] Intermittent-fasting and calorie-restriction trials in adults with overweight or obesity show associations with improved fasting glucose, fasting insulin, HOMA-IR, weight and blood pressure, mostly supported by very low or low quality evidence. This indicates that fasting glucose and insulin resistance are modifiable markers when weight is reduced. - PMID:34919135

[C | emerging] Reviews of the amlodipine/atorvastatin single pill describe amlodipine as the blood-pressure-lowering component and atorvastatin as the lipid-lowering component. Any lipid improvement on this combination is therefore attributed to the statin. - PMID:17380213

[C | evidence supported] Secondary hypercholesterolemia causes named by the consensus are hypothyroidism, liver disease, primary biliary cholangitis (a cholestatic condition) and nephrotic syndrome. The consensus recommends that all patients with high LDL-C be screened for these conditions. If cholesterol stays high after the underlying disease is managed, further lipid-lowering therapy may be required. - PMID:39252486

[C | evidence supported] The consensus lists screening laboratory tests for these causes: TSH and free T4 for hypothyroidism, transaminases, bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase for liver disease, and serum creatinine and urine/serum albumin for renal disease. It also lists fasting glucose/HbA1c for diabetes (listed under hypertriglyceridemia) and cortisol testing for Cushing syndrome (also listed under hypertriglyceridemia). - PMID:39252486

[C | evidence supported] Several drug classes can raise LDL-C: thiazides, steroid hormones (progestogens, androgenic steroids, glucocorticoids), dermatologic drugs, immunosuppressants such as cyclosporine, protease inhibitors and anticonvulsants. The consensus advises replacing the causative drug where possible, or monitoring lipids and reassessing the need for the drug if replacement is difficult. - PMID:39252486

[C | evidence supported] Diabetes, uncontrolled diabetes, obesity, chronic kidney disease and alcohol are named as secondary contributors to hypertriglyceridemia, and diet can also raise cholesterol. These are relevant to the overall lipid picture but are mainly triglyceride rather than LDL-C causes. - PMID:39252486

[C | evidence supported] A 1998 review gives the diabetes FPG cut-off as 7 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) or higher and describes diagnosis by two abnormal fasting plasma determinations. This is a historical source and may not reflect current ADA/WHO wording. - PMID:9803200

[C | emerging] The IDF position statement says a 1-hour post-load glucose of 209 mg/dL (11.6 mmol/L) or higher should be repeated to confirm type 2 diabetes. This supports the principle of repeat confirmation, but it applies to the 1-hour OGTT criterion, not to FPG. - PMID:38458916

[C | evidence supported] In a network meta-analysis of 22 RCTs, no statin, including atorvastatin, differed significantly from placebo or from other statins in new-onset diabetes risk. Fasting glucose and HbA1c also did not differ significantly. Point estimates varied by agent and dose, with substantial uncertainty. (verified with caveat) - PMID:42890578

[C | evidence supported] A literature review concluded that statin use is possibly associated with incident diabetes, mainly in patients with underlying diabetes risk factors. It advised monitoring for incident diabetes in patients on statins. - PMID:24849689

[C | hypothesis] A narrative review states that atorvastatin, simvastatin and rosuvastatin have the most pronounced diabetogenic properties. It also states that statin users with major T2DM risk factors, including glycemic parameters approaching the diabetes threshold, are at higher risk of developing diabetes. - PMID:42583924

[C | emerging] The same narrative review states that statin use should not be discouraged because cardiovascular benefit is judged to exceed the glycemic risk. It recommends glucose monitoring alongside continued statin treatment. - PMID:42583924

[C | emerging] A narrative review reports that South Asian individuals develop type 2 diabetes at younger ages and lower BMIs. Its authors support a lower BMI threshold for screening and measurement of postprandial glucose, but the abstract states no numeric glycaemic thresholds or screening intervals. - PMID:42935579

[C | emerging] South Asian populations are described as having a distinct metabolic profile, with beta-cell dysfunction at lower BMI, insulin resistance, lower lean mass and higher visceral adiposity. Standard diagnostic tools may fail to identify these individuals. - PMID:42935579

[C | emerging] A UK-based Norwegian study of women after gestational diabetes found that normoglycaemic South Asian women had lower insulin secretion for a given insulin resistance and lower hepatic insulin clearance than Nordic women. This suggests ethnic differences in insulin resistance and beta-cell compensation at similar glycaemia. - PMID:36112815

[C | emerging] In South Asian women after GDM, normoglycaemic women showed higher adipose tissue insulin resistance, inflammation markers and liver fat score than Nordic women. Liver fat score explained most of the ethnic difference in post-prandial glucose. - PMID:38786765

[C | emerging] In a South Asian cohort, data-driven subtypes of prediabetes and T2D differed in mortality. Insulin-deficient prediabetes was associated with higher all-cause and CVD mortality, whereas insulin-resistant prediabetes was not. Risk therefore depends on the pathophysiological subtype, not just the glycaemic category. - PMID:42102359

[C | emerging] The triglyceride-to-HDL ratio, a proposed surrogate for insulin resistance, was associated with insulin resistance in South Asian men but not in South Asian women in a UK multi-ethnic cohort. The study did not examine hypertension. - PMID:23251403

[C | evidence supported] The 2026 ACC/AHA guideline reintroduces explicit LDL-C, non-HDL-C and apoB treatment goals in select primary-prevention patients, based on risk category. The excerpts do not show the numeric values. - PMID:42295619

[C | evidence supported] The 2026 guideline defines PREVENT-ASCVD 10-year risk categories as low (<3%), borderline (3% to <5%), intermediate (5% to <10%) and high (≥10%). These are the categories by which primary-prevention goals are stratified. - PMID:42795336

[C | evidence supported] A secondary review reports convergence between the US and European frameworks on LDL-C goals below 70 mg/dL in high-risk and below 55 mg/dL in very-high-risk patients. Its excerpt does not specify which of these apply to primary prevention by PREVENT category, and it gives no non-HDL-C values. - PMID:42795336

[C | evidence supported] For clinical ASCVD at very high risk (secondary prevention), the guideline recommends LDL-C <55 mg/dL and non-HDL-C <85 mg/dL. This is not a primary-prevention goal but shows how paired LDL-C and non-HDL-C targets are expressed. - PMID:42709273

[C | evidence supported] No provided source gives LDL-C or non-HDL-C goals specific to adults with hypertension. Among the conditions that independently support LDL-lowering therapy, the excerpt lists diabetes, stage 3-4 CKD and HIV, not hypertension. - PMID:42795336

[C | evidence supported] A 2026 review of the ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline says the guideline emphasizes structured lipid monitoring. The supplied text does not give the testing intervals or timing. - PMID:42709273
[C | guideline supported] The 2025 VA/DoD guideline removed its earlier recommendation against routine lipid monitoring. The synopsis abstract does not specify an interval. - PMID:42735406

[C | emerging] The meta-analysis of ARB/amlodipine/rosuvastatin triple therapy versus ARB/amlodipine found a large LDL-C reduction. This comparison adds a statin, so it does not isolate any amlodipine effect on lipids and is not placebo-controlled for amlodipine. - PMID:41697569

[C | evidence supported] Secondary sources report the ADA-based FPG range for prediabetes (impaired fasting glucose) as 100 to 125 mg/dL and the diabetes threshold as 126 mg/dL or higher. The diabetes diagnosis is stated to need confirmation according to standard criteria. - PMID:42729512, PMID:42881653

[C | evidence supported] A supplied review states that WHO and ADA classification systems both define prediabetes and diabetes purely by glucose thresholds (fasting glucose, OGTT, HbA1c). It gives no WHO numeric FPG cut-offs and does not describe any WHO-ADA difference. - PMID:42930797

[C | evidence supported] The International Expert Committee advice, as summarised in a 2010 review, bases confirmation on a repeat HbA1c. It reserves FPG, 2-hour glucose and OGTT for situations where HbA1c cannot be used (assay unavailable, patient factors preventing interpretation, or pregnancy). It advises against mixing methods. This source does not describe confirmation of an isolated abnormal FPG by repeating FPG. - PMID:20150843

[C | evidence supported] The same 2010 review states that HbA1c alone can carry systematic error. It recommends combining HbA1c with plasma glucose for diagnosis and performing plasma glucose testing when an HbA1c result is discordant with the clinical picture or equivocal. This supports using a second test type in some circumstances. - PMID:20150843

[C | emerging] A 2026 cross-sectional study in 203 community-dwelling Thai adults aged 60 or older found FPG- and HbA1c-based glycaemic classifications to be only partly concordant. The authors concluded that discordant single measurements warrant confirmation and review of biological, analytical and treatment-related influences. They stated that the study does not establish that routine dual testing improves diagnosis or outcomes. - PMID:42942185

[C | evidence supported] A systematic review of long-term (≥1 year) CCB use in hypertension reported that several studies found a marginal increase in new-onset diabetes. The class-level association was not consistently demonstrated. - PMID:41873338

[C | emerging] In comparisons with angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), amlodipine was associated with a higher rate of new-onset diabetes. The difference reflects lower risk with ARBs relative to amlodipine rather than proof that amlodipine raises risk versus no treatment. - PMID:15526243, PMID:41873338

[C | emerging] In a retrospective observational study of patients on RAAS blockers, regimens with a thiazide or thiazide-like diuretic had a less favorable metabolic profile (higher triglyceride-glucose index) than regimens with a CCB. This suggests CCBs were relatively metabolically favorable compared with thiazides, not that they have no glycaemic effect. - PMID:42701822

[C | evidence supported] A 2026 Bayesian network meta-analysis of 22 RCTs found no statistically significant differences in new-onset diabetes risk across statin types and doses or versus placebo. Atorvastatin 80 mg/day had a relatively higher point estimate. Glycemic markers (FPG, HbA1c) also did not differ significantly. In patients without diabetes, HbA1c did not exceed 6.5% during statin treatment. (verified with caveat) - PMID:42890578

[C | emerging] In a Korean nationwide secondary-prevention cohort (29,826 patients with ASCVD), new-onset diabetes incidence was comparable between high- and moderate-intensity statins. Risk differed by individual statin, suggesting an agent-specific rather than uniform class effect. - PMID:41884637

[C | evidence supported] Narrative reviews describe atorvastatin as a higher-risk statin for new-onset diabetes. Risk is said to be greater in people with prediabetes, obesity or other metabolic risk factors, or glycemic parameters approaching the diabetes threshold. They advise glucose monitoring alongside continued statin therapy, because cardiovascular benefit is generally judged to outweigh the diabetes risk. - PMID:41809229, PMID:42583924

[C | evidence supported] Statin use is associated with an increased risk of new-onset type 2 diabetes in general populations. This background statement gives no South Asian-specific estimate. - PMID:41965920

[C | emerging] A large US retrospective cohort reports that HbA1c thresholds for predicting major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) vary by race/ethnicity and sex. South Asian individuals had a threshold in the prediabetic range, 6.0%-6.2%. These are risk-prediction thresholds from a Youden index, not diagnostic cut-offs for diabetes, and the authors state that no ethnicity-specific diagnostic thresholds exist. - PMID:38761085

[C | emerging] In South Asian adults, insulin-deficient prediabetes (IDPD) was associated with higher all-cause and CVD mortality than normal glucose tolerance, whereas insulin-resistant prediabetes was not. Prediabetes is therefore heterogeneous in this population, and glycemia thresholds alone may not capture risk. - PMID:42102359

[D | emerging] A 1984 review reported that antihypertensive drug classes can alter plasma lipids. Thiazides raise triglycerides and VLDL with little effect on TC, and non-selective beta-blockers raise triglycerides and lower HDL. It recommended measuring lipids before starting antihypertensive therapy and re-checking lipoprotein fractions during long-term therapy. Amlodipine, the patient's antihypertensive, is not covered by the source. - PMID:6143851

[D | hypothesis] Insulin-sensitivity indices such as QUICKI, which need fasting insulin and glucose, have been used with a cut-off below 0.35 as indicating possible insulin resistance. In a small cohort, differences in fasting glucose and QUICKI did not survive multiple-comparison correction. - PMID:42667517

[D | hypothesis] Early beta-cell dysfunction may be measurable (for example by intact proinsulin) while fasting glucose, HbA1c and OGTT are still within normal criteria. This 'normoglycemic diabetes' concept is explicitly hypothesis-generating and not an established diagnosis. - PMID:42930797

[D | emerging] Possible confounders and context for fasting glucose. In randomised trials in people without diabetes, higher dairy record was associated with slightly higher fasting glucose (mean difference 0.07 mmol/L) but lower HbA1c, so the two measures can diverge. In a large cross-sectional workforce study, elevated anxiety symptoms were associated with impaired fasting glucose and other cardiometabolic abnormalities. - PMID:30657868

[D | emerging] In a small retrospective study, patients on RAAS blocker plus a CCB had lower triglycerides and TyG index than those on RAAS blocker plus a thiazide-type diuretic. This shows a difference between regimens, not a lipid effect of amlodipine, and the CCB was not identified as amlodipine. - PMID:42701822
[D | hypothesis] Amlodipine's reported anti-atherosclerotic actions come from animal and cell work and are not evidence of a change in blood lipid levels. - PMID:9488196

[D | hypothesis] Spontaneous adverse-event reporting (FAERS) shows a disproportionate signal for hyperglycemic events with atorvastatin among patients without diabetes. This is a reporting-based signal, not an incidence or causal estimate. - PMID:42890578

[D | emerging] In a retrospective cohort of patients with new-onset type 2 diabetes, statin initiation was associated with less short-term glycemic improvement and a lower MACE risk. This illustrates the benefit-risk trade-off, but the population differs from this patient. - PMID:42729193

[D | emerging] In a small retrospective cohort of older adults with ASCVD, atorvastatin 20 mg/day was associated with a higher rate of new-onset diabetes than pitavastatin 4 mg/day over 12 months. - PMID:42528438

[D | hypothesis] A case report discussion notes that Indian consensus guidance sets a lower BMI cut-off for obesity in South Asians (BMI 25 or above), so a BMI classed as overweight by Western criteria may be obesity-range for this population. - PMID:42756621

[D | hypothesis] The TOMHS abstract describes an RCT arm of amlodipine versus placebo with lipid profile as an outcome. The abstract reports lipid results only for acebutolol, so the effect of amlodipine on LDL-C, triglycerides or HDL-C cannot be determined from the supplied text. - PMID:2220651

[D | hypothesis] When HbA1c is known to be unreliable, a 2026 case report advises relying on glucose-based criteria and direct glucose measurement rather than HbA1c. This is relevant only if a reason for HbA1c unreliability (for example a haemoglobin variant) is suspected. - PMID:42757138

[D | hypothesis] Pharmacovigilance data show disproportionate reporting of hyperglycaemia with amlodipine relative to several comparators, but reports of type 2 diabetes were less frequent. The authors state this cannot be read as clinical risk. - PMID:42653674

[D | hypothesis] In western-diet-fed mice, higher atorvastatin doses impaired glucose tolerance while a low dose did not, with associated beta-cell autophagy and loss. This is a mechanistic hypothesis and cannot be translated into human dose guidance. - PMID:38253121

[D | hypothesis] A hypothesis paper proposes that South Asians have a higher likelihood of statin-associated new-onset diabetes regardless of statin potency. The cited abstract gives no data, and this is an untested proposal, not an established effect. - PMID:25648661

[D | hypothesis] A 2026 editorial states that translation of statin safety findings to South Asian patients is a reasonable hypothesis that has not been directly tested. The pooled trial data it discusses were not reported by ethnic subgroup. - PMID:42898938

[D | hypothesis] A sub-Saharan African cross-sectional study found that a fasting plasma glucose cut-off of 105 mg/dL optimised detection of diabetes against the 2-hour OGTT value. This is population-specific evidence and is not from South Asian adults. - PMID:40206599
[E | hypothesis] The TOMHS abstract lists an amlodipine arm, but the lipid results it reports are for acebutolol only, so the abstract gives no amlodipine lipid effect. - PMID:2220651

items: [B | evidence supported] Pooled RCT data in CKD (mean eGFR about 55, mostly type 2 diabetes, hypertension and heart failure) show SGLT2 inhibitors versus placebo were associated with a placebo-subtracted annualized total eGFR slope difference of about +0.97 mL/min/1.73 m2/year (95% CI 0.34 to 1.59). The chronic-slope difference was +1.92. ESKD risk was lower (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.75). - PMID:42741446

[B | evidence supported] A meta-analysis restricted to diabetic CKD found no statistically significant eGFR difference (MD 0.25 mL/min/1.73 m2) and no significant UACR difference with SGLT2 inhibitors versus placebo. The authors describe these as neutral short- to medium-term surrogate effects, to be read alongside the large outcome trials. - PMID:42826278

[B | evidence supported] The pooled SGLT2-inhibitor safety signals in CKD included higher risks of diabetic ketoacidosis (RR 2.06) and volume depletion (RR 1.28), with fewer serious adverse events overall (RR 0.92). - PMID:42741446

[B | evidence supported] The KFRE has been validated with high discrimination across 31 multinational cohorts of people with CKD stages 3-5. Calibration was adequate in North America but sometimes overestimated risk elsewhere. - PMID:26757465

[B | guideline supported] The 2026 CKM guideline recommends staging by assessing metabolic risk factors, kidney function (eGFR) and CVD status. It recommends adding UACR assessment in CKM stage 2 and above and at least annual eGFR and UACR in those stages. This supports measuring albuminuria to determine this patient's risk stratum, but the excerpt shown contains no recommendation on SGLT2 or RAS inhibitor effects on eGFR slope in non-diabetic, normo-albuminuric adults. - PMID:42265997

[B | evidence supported] In SPRINT with long-term EHR follow-up, intensive SBP lowering was associated with a steeper eGFR slope and more eGFR-decline events during the intervention phase. This was not seen after the trial ended. In participants without CKD at baseline, the ≥30% eGFR-decline hazard ratio was 3.27 during the intervention. - PMID:37883184

[B | evidence supported] A post hoc analysis of SPRINT and ACCORD-BP found that intensive BP control did not increase kidney failure. In participants with baseline CKD, renal failure risk was lower (HR 0.46). The risk of ≥30% eGFR reduction was increased with or without CKD. Increased progression was limited to moderate- or high-risk KDIGO categories, not the very-high-risk category. - PMID:41117098

[C | evidence supported] Urate-lowering with allopurinol did not change measured GFR (PERL, difference 0.001 mL/min/1.73 m2) or annual eGFR decline (CKD-FIX, difference -0.10) versus placebo. The review concludes urate-lowering therapy should not be started solely for renoprotection in unselected CKD. - PMID:42688589

[C | evidence supported] The validation populations were mostly older adults with moderately reduced eGFR. Young adults and very low eGFR strata are not characterised in the excerpted text, so applicability there is unverified. - PMID:26757465

[C | evidence supported] KFRE calibration can be poor in specific clinical subpopulations. In people with multimorbidity, risk was under-estimated in one cohort, and a competing-mortality-adjusted model improved calibration. - PMID:41288315

[C | emerging] In general-population cohorts without known kidney disease (median baseline eGFR 84, mostly older US adults), the least-squares mean eGFR slope was about -1.15 mL/min/1.73 m2 per year in participants without clonal hematopoiesis. This is a mixed-treatment, non-South Asian reference point, not an untreated hypertensive slope. - PMID:36241009

[C | emerging] In a Japanese working-age screening cohort (mean age about 50, without prior AF or cardiovascular comorbidity), the annual eGFR decline in matched individuals who did not develop AF was about -0.94 mL/min/1.73 m2 per year. This is another indirect, non-South Asian, non-hypertension-specific estimate. - PMID:42133311

[C | emerging] Higher long-term systolic BP burden and BP variability were associated with faster eGFR decline in adults with preserved kidney function. A 1-SD higher cumulative SBP corresponded to roughly 0.15-0.18 mL/min/1.73 m2 per year additional decline. This gives a relative increment, not an absolute untreated slope. - PMID:42223339

[C | evidence supported] A systematic review of four trials and post hoc analyses reports that the relative risk of ≥40% eGFR decline under intensive control was higher in non-albuminuric patients. It concludes that intensive control does not cause long-term renal harm and that early eGFR decline may be hemodynamic. Patients with albuminuria appeared to gain the most renal benefit. - PMID:41035575

[C | evidence supported] The KFRE was validated in a large pooled meta-analysis of CKD stage 3-5 cohorts, with high overall discrimination. The excerpts give no eGFR-stratified results for G5 (eGFR <15). This supports the equation's stated scope but does not show accuracy specifically in G5. - PMID:26757465, PMID:41862268

[C | evidence supported] KFRE discrimination was similar across age, race and diabetes subgroups. Calibration was adequate in North American cohorts but overestimated risk in some non-North American cohorts, and a regional calibration factor was needed there. These are calibration limits in the CKD 3-5 population, not G5-specific findings. - PMID:26757465

[C | emerging] Observational data show the KFRE can miscalibrate in people with multimorbidity because it ignores competing mortality (risk under-estimated in UK Biobank, O/E 1.75 at 5 years). A competing-risk model improved calibration. This is relevant to interpreting KFRE accuracy generally but is not specific to eGFR <15. - PMID:41288315

[C | emerging] The trial evidence cited in the sources for non-diabetic patients comes from CKD populations (DAPA-CKD). Early cardiovascular outcome trials enrolled patients with relatively well-preserved kidney function but were conducted in type 2 diabetes and targeted people at high cardiovascular risk. Neither population matches a non-diabetic adult without albuminuria. - PMID:33197224

[C | emerging] A narrative review reports that SGLT2 inhibitor nephroprotection is seen despite an initial eGFR decline. It describes this as a predictable hemodynamic response, not structural kidney injury. This bears on how an early eGFR change should be read, but it is not a measured slope in non-albuminuric non-diabetic adults. - PMID:42940063

This does not show a lack of effect, because exposure was limited and the design was observational. - PMID:42942488

items: [B | evidence supported] Prediabetes classification depends on which measure is used (IFG, IGT or HbA1c, with ADA or WHO cut-offs). The all-cause mortality association was stronger for IGT-defined than for HbA1c-defined prediabetes. This suggests the tests are not interchangeable, and the sources provide only limited data on HbA1c-defined prediabetes. - PMID:34718834

[B | evidence supported] FIB-4 has imperfect accuracy against VCTE in a general-population cohort, with many people misclassified as low or high risk. Misclassification was more likely in people with prediabetes/diabetes. - PMID:38428706

[B | evidence supported] A systematic review of discordance studies (15 studies, 593,354 participants, including statin-treated and untreated patients) found apoB to be a more accurate marker of atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk than LDL-C in all 9 studies that compared them. ApoB was also more accurate than non-HDL-C in most studies. This is an association with risk prediction, not proof that apoB-guided therapy improves outcomes. - PMID:40681368

[B | evidence supported] In 9,191 statin-treated patients with coronary artery disease, discordantly high apoB or high non-HDL-C with low LDL-C was associated with higher myocardial infarction risk. High LDL-C with low apoB or non-HDL-C was not. The association was seen in acute coronary syndrome but not in chronic coronary syndrome, and apoB showed no advantage over non-HDL-C. - PMID:38161343

[B | evidence supported] A systematic review and meta-analysis found HbA1c higher in IDA, in latent iron deficiency (LID, without anaemia), and in iron-deficient adults generally. HbA1c fell after iron therapy. Assay method and the anaemia and iron-deficiency definitions explained much of the heterogeneity. This is an association, and it concerns a laboratory measure rather than clinical outcomes. - PMID:42828220

[B | evidence supported] In prospective cohorts, intermediate hyperglycaemia (including a fasting glucose of 5.6 mmol/L or higher) was associated with later type 2 diabetes, but the certainty of the prognostic evidence was low. The Cochrane authors advise caution about active intervention in people labelled with intermediate hyperglycaemia. This is background for why an accurate classification matters, not a statement about iron status. - PMID:30371961

[C | emerging] In adults with type 2 diabetes in China, elevated LDL-C was associated with CKD, and dyslipidaemia, glycaemic control and CKD co-occur. This is association only and does not identify a cause of this patient's raised total cholesterol; it does suggest glycaemic and kidney status are relevant context (the patient's fasting glucose is 5.8 mmol/L, above the reference range). - PMID:39213031

[C | evidence supported] Guideline-eligibility modelling shows LDL-C thresholds (e.g., 190 mg/dL or higher), diabetes and CKD as criteria for statin eligibility independent of risk estimation, which makes LDL-C level, diabetes status and CKD status the relevant data points for management, but this is not a work-up for cause. - PMID:42475062

[C | evidence supported] The ADA defines prediabetes by three alternative glycaemic measures: HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose and 2-hour OGTT glucose. These are the primary tests for characterising an abnormal fasting glucose result. - PMID:42796348

[C | emerging] MASLD is described as interacting bidirectionally with cardiovascular, renal and metabolic dysfunction, so liver assessment is part of a cardiometabolic work-up. The excerpt does not show the fibrosis-risk (FIB-4) thresholds. - PMID:42796348

[C | guideline supported] The Endocrine Society guideline recommends that patients with hypertriglyceridemia be evaluated for secondary causes of hyperlipidemia. The abstract does not specify which tests to use, and it addresses hypertriglyceridemia rather than LDL-C elevation. - PMID:22962670

[C | evidence supported] Total cholesterol on a statin cannot be attributed to LDL-C, triglycerides or Lp(a) from the available data. The reviews list several non-LDL contributors to residual risk, so the partition would change interpretation. The high-sensitivity C-reactive protein of 2.1 mg/L (reference <3.0) is not elevated. - PMID:42865594

[C | evidence supported] Lp(a) is an LDL-C-independent contributor to risk. High concentrations are associated with ASCVD risk even at low LDL-C, and statins generally do not lower Lp(a). If Lp(a) is the main contributor to the cholesterol excess, the statin dose or type would not be expected to address it. - PMID:33257928

[C | emerging] In a UK Biobank cohort of statin-treated adults with established ASCVD or type 2 diabetes, moderately elevated Lp(a) (upper tertile, >46.8 nmol/L) was associated with higher MACE risk. The association was stronger in people without established ASCVD. This is an association, not proof of causation. - PMID:42240227

[C | evidence supported] A Mendelian randomization-informed review concludes that cardiovascular risk is particle-centric (ApoB) rather than LDL-C-centric, and that remnant cholesterol, not triglyceride per se, drives ASCVD risk in familial hypertriglyceridemia. It also states that LDL-C alone is insufficient as a diagnostic criterion for FH in adults and is confounded by age, lifestyle and Lp(a). This supports looking at ApoB, remnant cholesterol and Lp(a) when LDL-C alone does not explain the profile. - PMID:42512800

[C | emerging] A narrative review argues HbA1c is unreliable as a standalone diagnostic test in South Asian populations because of anaemia, haemoglobin variants, G6PD deficiency and poorly standardised assays. It lists specific mechanisms by which HbA1c can read falsely low or falsely high. - PMID:41743216

[C | emerging] The same review advises a multiparametric, risk-stratified approach rather than HbA1c alone. This approach includes OGTT, self-monitoring of blood glucose, CGM where possible, and haematological assessment. It does not name a single preferred confirmatory test for IFG. - PMID:41743216

[C | emerging] South Asian studies comparing HbA1c with glucose-based tests give heterogeneous results. One South Indian study found high HbA1c sensitivity and specificity at 6.5% for diabetes. A Bangladeshi study suggested lower HbA1c cut-offs. A Singapore study found a different HbA1c-glucose relationship in Indians and Malays than in Chinese. These studies address diabetes or prediabetes in general, not isolated IFG confirmation. - PMID:41743216

[C | emerging] In a non-South Asian population (Ethiopia and Nigeria), FPG and 2-h plasma glucose agreed only moderately for prediabetes and diabetes. FPG missed a substantial proportion of cases found by the 2-h glucose. This indirectly suggests that FPG, OGTT and HbA1c may classify the same person differently. - PMID:40206599

[C | evidence supported] An umbrella review of systematic reviews reports that statins, particularly atorvastatin and rosuvastatin, are associated with increased risk of new-onset diabetes. Pitavastatin may be protective. This is an association from reviews mostly rated critically low in confidence, not proof that atorvastatin caused this patient's glucose value. - PMID:42582540

[C | evidence supported] The Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' Collaboration, as summarised in the umbrella review, reported increased odds of worsening glycaemia with both low/moderate-intensity and high-intensity statins, with a larger estimate for high intensity. - PMID:42582540

[C | emerging] The umbrella review reports a diabetes-risk signal specifically for atorvastatin, including the 80 mg dose, with considerable heterogeneity in some analyses. Pitavastatin was associated with a lower diabetes risk than atorvastatin in one cited comparison. - PMID:42582540

[C | evidence supported] A review of type 2 diabetes dyslipidaemia states that the minor glycaemia increase seen in statin trials does not impair the beneficial cardiovascular results. The glycaemic signal should therefore be weighed against cardiovascular benefit rather than treated in isolation. - PMID:41143728

[C | evidence supported] A stepwise pathway is recommended for at-risk populations: FIB-4 first, then VCTE or ELF as second-line non-invasive testing. This is described as contemporary guidance in a narrative review and is applied to type 2 diabetes in an endocrinology pathway proposal. - PMID:42597408, PMID:42942568

[C | evidence supported] Normal liver enzymes do not reliably exclude significant or advanced fibrosis, so enzyme-triggered investigation alone can give false reassurance in people with metabolic risk. - PMID:42942568

[C | emerging] Higher fibrosis tier on guideline-based non-invasive pathways (FIB-4 followed by VCTE) was associated with incident ASCVD in patients with prediabetes. The association was not evident in people with diabetes. - PMID:42520169

[C | evidence supported] The 2026 ACC/AHA multisociety guideline, as summarised in a 2026 review table, recommends one-time Lp(a) measurement in all adults (COR 1, LOE B-NR). This applies regardless of statin use. - PMID:42676490, PMID:42818569

[C | evidence supported] An Lp(a) of at least 125 nmol/L (50 mg/dL) is classed as risk-enhancing, and higher values carry graded risk. In the guideline's staged approach, risk-enhancing factors and selective CAC are considered after PREVENT calculation, so an elevated Lp(a) could move a patient to a higher risk category. - PMID:42795336, PMID:42818569

[C | evidence supported] Statins and other conventional lipid-lowering therapies do not reduce Lp(a) meaningfully. Lp(a) is a largely genetically determined, causal contributor to residual cardiovascular risk despite LDL-C lowering, so statin treatment does not make Lp(a) irrelevant. - PMID:42818569

[C | emerging] It is not established that lowering Lp(a) reduces cardiovascular events. Outcome trials of RNA-targeted agents, for example pelacarsen in established ASCVD, had results pending at the literature cut-off, and no Lp(a)-lowering drug is shown to improve outcomes. Management after a high Lp(a) therefore relies on intensifying conventional risk-factor control. - PMID:42818569

[C | evidence supported] An elevated Lp(a) is described as prompting comprehensive risk-factor intensification and, where appropriate, family-based evaluation. Reviews describe early intensification of therapy, addition of non-statin agents, and CAC scoring to resolve borderline risk. The sources do not specify what Lp(a) level triggers a change in statin intensity or an add-on agent. - PMID:42629510, PMID:42676490

[C | evidence supported] Lp(a) assay standardisation is incomplete. Mass (mg/dL) and molar (nmol/L) units are not interchangeable, and some immunoassays are biased by apolipoprotein(a) isoform size. The guideline reportedly favours isoform-insensitive, traceable assays. - PMID:42818569

[C | emerging] In a Hong Kong peripheral artery disease cohort (n=3,847), higher early cumulative non-HDL-C exposure was associated with higher cardiovascular death, including among individuals with well-controlled LDL-C. Patients with high non-HDL-C despite low LDL-C had the highest risk of cardiovascular death. Non-HDL-C added a modest improvement in model discrimination over LDL-C. - PMID:42968163

[C | evidence supported] Statin therapy lowers LDL-C more than LDL-P or apoB, so apoB and LDL-P can remain at higher population percentiles when LDL-C appears well treated. This supports a mechanistic basis for discordance and residual risk, but outcome data were sparse. - PMID:23893306

[C | evidence supported] Recent guideline comparisons place non-HDL-C as a co-primary target in the 2026 ACC/AHA framework and describe apoB as recommended in discordance or as a refiner of risk, with growing emphasis on apoB. A critical review notes the recommendations rest on a non-uniform evidence base, with some supported by observational data or surrogate endpoints and ApoB-guided treatment still uncertain. - PMID:42180797, PMID:42795336

[C | emerging] In a population free of ASCVD and not on statins (MESA), apoB was associated with coronary calcium but added only modest predictive value beyond LDL-C or non-HDL-C. This tempers the case for incremental value from apoB. - PMID:31882375

[C | evidence supported] Triglycerides and their remnant lipoproteins are described as contributors to residual cardiovascular risk that persists when LDL-C is well controlled. The evidence is observational, Mendelian-randomisation and mechanistic, so the strength of causality remains debated. - PMID:42151489, PMID:42243955
[C | evidence supported] Prospective cohort and trial-analysis data show that remnant cholesterol and on-statin TG predict cardiovascular events beyond LDL-C and apoB. - PMID:42151489

[C | emerging] Atherogenicity of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins appears driven mainly by the cholesterol they carry (remnant cholesterol) rather than by triglyceride itself. Reviews also note that TG-lowering trials with fibrates and omega-3 products did not consistently reduce events. - PMID:36924359, PMID:42609715

[C | evidence supported] Cardiovascular benefit in trials of TG-targeted therapies is described as tracking reductions in non-HDL-C and apoB more closely than TG lowering. Guidelines recommend evaluating non-HDL-C, which captures remnant and other atherogenic particles. - PMID:37641208, PMID:42325672

[C | evidence supported] Icosapent ethyl is described as the only TG-related therapy with a significant reduction in major cardiovascular events in a large RCT. The EMA-approved indication is limited to statin-treated patients with elevated TG and established CV disease, or diabetes plus another risk factor. - PMID:35304222

[C | emerging] An IDF consensus position statement argues that the 1-h post-load plasma glucose predicts diabetes and complications better than FPG, HbA1c or 2-h PG, and may reduce misclassification when FPG or HbA1c alone are used. It does not rank repeat FPG, 2-h OGTT and HbA1c for confirming IFG, and it is a proposal to add a test rather than an established standard. - PMID:38458916

[C | evidence supported] In non-diabetic adults, a second systematic review found the effect of IDA on HbA1c inconsistent in direction and magnitude. The primary pooled analysis was inconclusive. IDA may nonetheless cause HbA1c-based misclassification near diagnostic thresholds, so HbA1c should be read cautiously, especially when it disagrees with glucose-based tests. - PMID:42798745

[C | emerging] Iron correction may lower HbA1c without any true glycaemic improvement. A narrative framework suggests confirming iron deficiency with a blood count and iron indices, and using laboratory glucose for diagnosis rather than intensifying therapy from HbA1c alone. The authors state the framework is not a validated guideline. - PMID:42745822

[C | emerging] Narrative reviews report that HbA1c is unreliable when red-cell lifespan or glycation is perturbed (renal failure, haemolytic anaemia, haemoglobin variants, iron deficiency). Alternatives such as glycated albumin may be preferred in these settings but have their own failure modes. - PMID:42779420

[D | hypothesis] Among adults with CKD, nephrotic-range disease and diabetes are described as contexts in which lipid abnormalities occur, but the sources give no validated test panel to discriminate causes of raised total cholesterol. In a paediatric congenital nephrotic syndrome cohort, hypercholesterolemia was frequent alongside heavy proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia (an indirect pointer to urine protein and albumin assessment; not applicable to this adult). - PMID:42770105

[D | emerging] In kidney transplant recipients, FPG and HbA1c are reported to miss early post-transplant diabetes, and OGTT is described as valuable. This is a transplant-specific cause of dysglycaemia. It does not apply to this patient, who has no reported transplant or immunosuppression. - PMID:38558257

[D | emerging] A 2026 narrative review lists differentiation between primary and secondary causes as part of the initial evaluation of elevated LDL-C. The abstract and excerpt provided do not identify the tests involved. - PMID:42203447

[D | hypothesis] A narrative review's educational vignette describes standardized confirmation, verification of medication exposure and etiological assessment for persistent dyslipidemia. Its tables show that liver function tests, TSH and inflammatory markers were measured in that illustrative case. This is a single example, not a recommendation. - PMID:42807810

[D | hypothesis] A proposed Romanian risk framework (ROMA-CV) embeds once-in-a-lifetime Lp(a) measurement and selective coronary calcium or ultrasound imaging into risk assessment. The authors state it is hypothesis-generating and not validated. - PMID:42513406

[D | emerging] In an adult cross-sectional study in Yemen, the prevalence of prediabetes differed substantially depending on the test used (FBS, OGTT or HbA1c). This supports poor concordance between tests. It does not show which test is preferred. - PMID:41597373

[D | hypothesis] A registered randomised trial protocol describes statin-associated dysglycaemia as a recognised concern and tests whether ursodeoxycholic acid can prevent it. The trial has no results yet and provides no evidence on amlodipine. - PMID:42521308

[D | hypothesis] In nondiabetic MASLD (mostly prediabetic), the metabolic syndrome phenotype was associated with FIB-4-defined fibrosis risk but not with age-independent FibroScan stiffness. This suggests FIB-4 findings in this population may partly reflect the age dependence of the score. The authors present this as hypothesis-generating. - PMID:42994828

[D | hypothesis] A 2026 narrative review describes a clinical vignette of persistent dyslipidaemia. It refers generally to verifying medication exposure and assessing etiology, without a defined list of tests in the shown excerpt. Its tables show TSH, liver tests and CRP were measured in the vignette, but these are descriptive, not recommendations. - PMID:42807810

[D | hypothesis] A case report of lorlatinib-associated dyslipidaemia notes that subclinical hypothyroidism was detected during follow-up and may have contributed to the lipid elevation. It calls for evaluation of secondary contributors but does not list specific tests. - PMID:42923625

[D | emerging] Fenofibrate added to a statin gave neutral overall cardiovascular outcomes. Prespecified subgroup analyses in patients with high TG suggest possible benefit, but these come mainly from type 2 diabetes trials and need confirmation. - PMID:42325672

[D | emerging] A narrative review reports that classification of prediabetes depends heavily on the test and threshold used, and that concordance among FPG, HbA1c and 2-h glucose is poor. Inter-ethnic variability is flagged as a source of controversy, but no South Asian figures are given in the excerpt. - PMID:42819525

[D | hypothesis] A 1998 review described diagnostic criteria based on fasting plasma glucose (FPG 126 mg/dL or higher) for diabetes. It predates current guidance and says nothing about confirming IFG, HbA1c or ancestry, so it cannot answer the question about current guideline preferences. - PMID:9803200

[D | hypothesis] Haemoglobin variants and related red-cell disorders can distort HbA1c, and the error can run falsely low or high depending on the variant and assay. The evidence here is one case report of a clinically silent alpha-globin variant giving a profoundly low HbA1c, plus a narrative review of South Asian settings. It does not quantify how often this occurs. - PMID:41743216, PMID:42757138
